title: Your Jira ticket belongs in the code review
text: Every pull request has two halves, the code and what the code was supposed to do. The second half usually lives in Jira (or another ticketing system), where you'll find the acceptance criteria, edge case someone flagged in a comment, and context a PM and an engineer worked out days before the diff was written. Reviewers, human or AI, rarely have that half in front of them. They see the diff. [CodeRabbit's Jira integration](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/connections/jira) closes that gap. Once it's connected, CodeRabbit pulls the linked issue straight into the review, so the same tool checking your code for bugs is also checking it against what you were actually asked to build and associates the proper priority that originates in Jira, which is closest to the customer. ## Reviews that understand why, not just what Link a Jira issue in your PR description, such as `Closes https://yourcompany.atlassian.net/browse/SCRUM-123`, and CodeRabbit fetches the issue's details before it reviews a single line. The review then accounts for the ticket's constraints instead of judging the diff in isolation. ## Acceptance criteria, checked automatically Beyond "does this compile," CodeRabbit reads the issue's acceptance criteria and flags any drift between the implementation and the requirement, such as a missed edge case, a criterion nobody implemented, or scope that quietly grew. The check used to depend on a reviewer keeping the ticket open in another tab and mapping each criterion onto the diff by hand. ## Initiate and complete the workflow from Slack Once CodeRabbit is connected to Jira and Slack, you can describe the work and ask CodeRabbit Agent to create a Jira issue, make the changes, and open a linked PR in GitHub. You can then ask the agent to address review feedback and failing checks to get the PR ready to merge. When the work is complete, you can also ask it to resolve the Jira issue, all without leaving Slack. Workflow initiation from Slack ## Turn a ticket into a coding plan CodeRabbit's Issue Planner generates a full, codebase-aware coding plan directly from a Jira issue, with research, step-by-step tasks, and agent-ready prompts. You, or your coding agent of choice, can go from the ticket to a concrete implementation plan without doing the research by hand. Comment `@coderabbitai plan` on any issue, or set up auto-planning to generate a plan whenever an issue matches rules you define, such as label, status, assignee, or issue type. ## File the follow-up without leaving the PR Found something worth tracking, but it’s out of scope for the current PR? Ask CodeRabbit to create the ticket right there by commenting `@coderabbitai create a Jira issue for this technical debt in the PROJ project`. It creates a well-structured issue with the context of the review, in the right project, and can even nest it as a subtask under an existing issue. No new tab, no retyping the finding. ## Set up once, at the repo level Open Connections in CodeRabbit and add a Jira connection. For reviews, Jira Cloud installs through the Atlassian Marketplace, and Jira Data Center uses a personal access token for self-hosted setups. Add the connection to your Review scope, which controls where CodeRabbit can use it, then set `knowledge_base.jira.project_keys` in `.coderabbit.yaml` to choose which Jira projects can provide review context. Jira context is on by default for private repositories. For the Slack workflow, pick a connection method that supports CodeRabbit Agent and enable it in the scope your Slack conversation uses. The animation below shows the OAuth connection flow. Learn more in the [Jira integration docs](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/connections/jira), or connect your Jira workspace from [Connections](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/connections) to [try it on your next PR](https://app.coderabbit.ai/login?free-trial=).
